opus-5.5.text:
I think the best way is honestly to try the models on the things you actually care about. Benchmarks are useful, and I spend a lot of my time building them, but the most meaningful signal for any individual person is whether the model helps with their real work. So if you're a lawyer, give it a real contract you'd review. If you're an engineer, hand it an actual bug from your codebase. If you're a researcher, ask it the hard question you've been stuck on.

What we've seen is that a lot of the classic academic benchmarks have saturated. Models went from struggling on them to basically acing them in a short time, so they stopped telling us much. That's part of why we've moved toward evaluations grounded in real-world, economically valuable tasks. The idea is to take work that experienced professionals across many occupations actually do, with realistic inputs and deliverables, and have experts compare the model's output to what a skilled human would produce. That tells you much more about whether a model is useful than whether it can answer a multiple-choice trivia question.

I'd also encourage people to keep a small personal set of prompts or tasks and rerun them whenever a new model comes out. It's a lightweight version of what we do internally, and it builds real intuition for how capabilities are changing, including where models still fall short. Pay attention to the failures too: where it's confidently wrong, where it needs a lot of hand-holding, where it can't finish a longer multi-step task. Those gaps are often where the next big improvements show up.

r001.rationale: The response says to try models on the things people actually care about and use them on real work, such as contracts, code bugs, and research questions.

r002.rationale: It recommends rerunning a personal set of tasks when a new model comes out, but does not specifically recommend retrying tasks the model handled poorly a week earlier.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the way we evaluate models has to keep changing, because the models keep changing what "hard" means.

A few years ago, you could hand a model a standardized test or a coding benchmark and learn a lot. Those were genuinely informative. But the problem with any fixed benchmark is that it saturates. Once models are getting ninety-plus percent, the test stops telling you anything about the frontier. So the first thing I'd say is: don't fall in love with a single number. If a benchmark has been around for a while and everyone is near the ceiling, treat it as a floor, not a measure of capability.

The second thing is to evaluate on tasks that look like the actual work you want done. That's the direction we've been pushing with things like real-world, expert-graded tasks, where you take work that a professional would actually be paid to do, have the model attempt it, and have experts in that field judge the output. It's expensive and slow, but it's much closer to the question people actually care about, which is: can this thing do something economically or scientifically useful, and how often does it fail?

Third, I'd pay a lot of attention to the shape of the failures, not just the pass rate. Two models can score the same and be completely different in practice. One fails by saying "I'm not sure," the other fails by confidently making something up. For most real uses, the second is far worse. So look at calibration, look at how the model behaves when it's out of its depth, look at whether it can tell you when it's uncertain.

And finally, for individuals and teams rather than researchers, I'd just say: build your own small eval. Take twenty or thirty examples of the thing you actually need, including the annoying edge cases, and run every new model against them. It takes an afternoon, and it's more predictive of your experience than any leaderboard. The public benchmarks are useful for tracking the field. Your own eval is what tells you whether to switch.

r001.rationale: The response recommends evaluating models on real work and on examples from the user’s own needs, identifying practical tasks as more informative than public benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It recommends rerunning a small custom evaluation against new models, but does not mention retrying tasks the model handled poorly a week earlier.

astra-6.text:
I think the best way is to evaluate them on things you actually want to do. Take a task you understand well, give the model the context it needs, and ask yourself: Is this useful? Is it correct? How much work do I have to do to get it to something I would actually use?

And try a range of examples, rather than drawing a conclusion from one impressive answer or one failure. If you keep a consistent set of tasks, you can come back to them as models improve and see where they’re making progress—and where you still need to check their work. Benchmarks can be helpful, but the most meaningful evaluation is whether a model helps you do your own work better.

r001.rationale: It recommends evaluating models on real tasks you want to do and judging whether they help with your own work.

r002.rationale: It suggests revisiting a consistent set of tasks as models improve, but does not specifically recommend retrying tasks the model handled poorly a week earlier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the best way is to start with what you actually want the model to do. Take real tasks from your work or your life, give different models the same task, and look carefully at the results. Did it get the answer right? Did it follow your instructions? How much back-and-forth did it take to get something useful?

Benchmarks can be helpful, but a single score won’t tell you whether a model is better for your particular use case. And as models improve, we need to keep updating our evaluations—include harder problems, look at where the models still fail, and test whether they can reliably complete an entire task rather than just one step.

r001.rationale: It recommends evaluating models on real tasks from your work or life and comparing how they perform.

r002.rationale: It recommends updating evaluations and examining failures, but does not say to retry poorly handled tasks a week later.
